Hacker News #9

Microsoft 365 outage leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests

Microsoft 365 outage leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests

科技产品 作者 DeepLogin 热度 639 回复 278 2026/11/16 02:36
打开原帖 打开外部链接 JSON

摘要

  • Diesem Problem waren wir alle ausgesetzt: Am Freitag gab es eine Störung, die den US-Softwarekonzern Microsoft lahmgelegt hat. Unter anderem das E-Mail-Programm Outlook. Betroffen war auch das Phantasialand. Durch die Störung kamen keine Mails an, wie das Unternehmen dem WDR am Samstag mitteilte. So bekam niemand mit, dass das Wartungssicherheitssystem der Saunalandschaft längst per Mail Alarm geschlagen hat. Denn das automatischen Dosiersystem hatte zu viel Chlor in den Pool gepumpt. Reizungen der Atemwege Dadurch wurden Gäste im Hotel Ling Bao des Phantasialands in Brühl verletzt. Sie haben über gesundheitliche Probleme geklagt, nachdem sie den Pool besucht hatten. Der wurde zeitweise gesperrt, konnte inzwischen aber wieder freigegeben werden, wie die Feuerwehr am Samstag dem WDR mitteilte. Wegen der Beschwerden der Hotel-Besucher wurden Rettungskräfte und die Feuerwehr gerufen. 13 Gäste klagten über Reizungen der Atemwege, letztlich stieg die Zahl der Betroffenen auf insgesamt 15. Überhöhter Chlorgehalt: Eine Person bleibt im Krankenhaus Zunächst hieß es, dass fünf Gäste ins Krankenhaus gebracht wurden, später wurde die Zahl auf vier korrigiert, eine Person davon blieb wegen einer mittelschweren Verletzung zur Beobachtung im Krankenhaus. Im Hotel ergaben Tests der Einsatzkräfte einen Defekt des automatischen Dosiersystems für den Pool. Dies hatte zu einem deutlich überhöhten Chlorgehalt geführt. Das Wasser wurde daher ausgetauscht. Betreiber der Mauritius-Therme wird hellhörig Die Nachricht über den Chlorunfall im Hotel im Phantasialand hat auch Max Wiesen, den Betreiber von "Mauritius Hotel und Therme", hellhörig werden lassen.
  • "Da denkt man natürlich immer selber: Oh je, kann uns das auch passieren?" Max Wiesen, Betreiber von "Mauritius Hotel und Therme"

amluto 2026/11/16 06:43
I personally operate a fairly advanced closed-loop chlorination system, and this is beyond screwed up.

These systems can easily fail, and they tend to fail in a way that causes them to measure low or zero chlorine and thus overdispense chlorine. More below on why.

First, this means that an operator must always ensure safety, both against excessive chlorine and against insufficient chlorine. In a commercial context, that means that a real human (or maybe a totally different sensor design, e.g. a colorimetric sensor) need to measure the pool chlorine level, preferably with a high quality titration (drop test) every day before opening the pool. They should probably record the result in pen on water resistant paper, but this part is icing on the cake.

Second, hoping that an email gets noticed is ridiculous. If you do not have positive confirmation that the pool is safe to open, don’t open it.

Third, the systems should be sized so that they cannot overdose quickly. The maximum dispensing rate should be such that hours of continuous operation would be required to reach an uncomfortable level, let alone a dangerous level. (Hot tubs are sort of an exception here.)

Fourth, everyone should be using a reasonable amount of CYA in their pool. Even at a lowish level of 30ppm CYA it takes a lot of chlorine to become dangerous unless the operator has also lost control of pH. I realize that some codes are confused about this.

Fifth, chlorine is smelly. Someone should have noticed, even just casually. Admittedly, lots of swimmers may be conditioned to stinky pools, and checking for safety isn’t their job. But the staff should notice.

Sixth, the systems I’ve seen beep when there’s an alert. It’s easy to add flashing lights, too. (In fact, the system I’m familiar with automatically shuts down if it feeds for more than X minutes without reaching the setpoint, and you cannot turn this feature off. You can, however, defeat it by switching the power to the whole controller.)

—- sensors —-

Actual free chlorine sensors intended for pools use an amperometric probe immersed in iodide solution or gel, separated from the pool water by a fancy membrane. Free chlorine oxidizes iodide to iodine, and the sensor measures the iodine concentration. If the membrane fails (or general wear and tear or excessive pressure swings) cause the iodide to be lost, then the chlorine can’t react and the sensor reads zero (or low if there’s tiny bit of iodide left).

Interestingly, these sensors are rather expensive devices that appear to mostly come from France and Germany. The Chinese vendors seem to be rebranding European parts (!), and the major US vendor is very clearly reselling a French company’s product.

There are some vendors who sell a cheap (or absurdly marked up) potentiometric ORP-based closed-loop system. In my considered opinion, these are worse than useless.

amluto 2026/11/16 06:59
Chlorine and chloramines have different smells. I find chlorine to have a cleanish smell and chloramines to smell nastier. (I don’t know precisely what compound I’m perceiving in the chloramine category. I think that monochloramine is likely almost odorless in the concentrations found in pools (this is one of the reasons it’s used in water distribution), so dichloramine and nitrogen trichloride are likely responsible for the stink.

Plain chlorine ought to be noticeable before it sends people to the hospital.

misswaterfairy 2026/11/16 18:31
> Plain chlorine ought to be noticeable before it sends people to the hospital.

One would have thought so, the story itself doesn't add up to me[1], perhaps it might be a translation issue?

Gaseous chlorine[2] systems for places like pools and hotels aren't all that common (I couldn't think of anywhere outside civil water treatment or major industrial), liquid chlorine (sodium hypochlorite [3]) chlorination systems are a lot more common because they're supposed to be relatively safer to operate.

Sodium hypochlorite is certainly much safer to handle compared to straight chlorine gas[4], but it will still give off the characteristic chlorine odour and will still happily hurt anyone not respecting it.

I wonder whether it was an absence of mind thing for patrons if the pool was indoor, the smell of chlorine tends to be stronger than outdoor pools? (enclosed setting, higher dosing given water warmth, etc.)

[1] Hazmat trained firefighter (though I am not a chemist)

[2] https://docs.airliquide.com.au/msdsau/AL640.pdf

[3] https://hyclor.com.au/downloads/msds-sheets/HY-CLOR_Liquid_C...

[4] Both have similar response requirements (Hazchem codes 2X, vs. 2XE), though chlorine gas releases demand much more extensive public safety measures (evacuation). See UN 3310 and 1791: https://www.ntc.gov.au/sites/default/files/assets/files/Aust...

amluto 2026/11/17 07:32
Indeed. If you have a spa and, every time you add chlorine, you have zero measurable free chlorine an hour later, you need more chlorine. Chlorine is not that reactive once it’s finished reacting with all the nasties that you want it to react with.

(There are plenty of subtleties. The troublefreepool “SLAM” protocol is a fairly good guide. If you have excessive CYA, you may need to change the water first. If you are using dichlor or trichlor, you may want to switch to liquid chlorine or make sure you’re doing adequate water changes. If you’re using liquid chlorine, make sure it’s not too old - it degrades over time, especially in hot climates. If you have too little CYA, especially if you like running the jets, you may lose chlorine faster than you like. If you don’t have the Taylor chlorine drop test kit, buy it.)

boie0025 2026/11/16 14:19
So long ago, in another life I worked at a pool company as a backstockist/deliverist. I brought chlorine tanks out to cars, delivered it to houses and dealt with all matters of chlorine. I am not a chemist, and that was about 28 years ago, but I can tell you that all of the things I handled smelled like pool. I realize that a lot of what I was smelling was spilled chemicals onto dirty stockroom floors, but the times I did have to open a fresh container -- I can tell you -- chlorine smells like chlorine. That said, I am talking about highly concentrated death liquid; but having gone to many a site to deliver this chemistry.. I guess my point is that we don't need piss for our noses to detect the presence of chlorine. In my experience.

EDIT: I want to add that if you breathe that crap long enough, it really makes everything else smell really weird/awful/chlorine-y. Until now I never thought to look it up, but the after effects of being around chlorine for a while leaves a distinct olfactory residue, and it is awful.
